title: Bilateral thalamic infarct involving artery of Percheron: a case report
case_prompt:
A 60-year-old woman with chronic hypertension was brought to the emergency department by her family after suddenly losing consciousness at home approximately 1 hour earlier. On arrival, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was E1V1M4. She had bilaterally dilated, nonreactive pupils (7 mm on the right, 5 mm on the left). She was intubated for airway protection. Initial vital signs were blood pressure 130/90 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats/min, oxygen saturation 85% on room air, and random blood glucose 158 mg/dL.

Neurologic examination revealed left-sided hemiplegia and left facial droop. The left plantar response was upgoing; the right was mute. Motor strength was 1/5 in the left upper and lower limbs and 2/5 on the right. There were no meningeal signs. Cardiovascular, pulmonary, and other systemic examinations were unremarkable.

A noncontrast head CT scan was obtained within 30 minutes of arrival.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Top-of-the-basilar artery syndrome was considered given bilateral thalamic involvement — “Bilateral thalamic infarcts due to embolic occlusion of arteries in the brainstem, including the PCA, superior cerebellar artery, and pontine arteries.”  
2. Cerebral venous thrombosis was considered because venous occlusion can cause bilateral thalamic lesions — “Occlusion of internal cerebral veins, such as the Vein of Galen and Straight Sinus, leads to isolated bilateral thalamic infarcts.”  
3. Chronic hypertensive encephalopathy was considered as a small-vessel cause — “Rare cases of chronic hypertension causing bilateral thalamic lacunar infarcts.”  
4. Infectious or inflammatory conditions were considered for bilateral thalamic lesions — “Tuberculosis, malaria, meningoencephalitis, and viral infections can cause bilateral paramedian thalamic lesions.”  
5. Neoplastic processes were considered because tumors can expand both thalami — “Bilateral thalamic glioma, a rare neoplastic condition, can result in bilateral thalamic expansion and hydrocephalus.”  
6. Demyelinating diseases were considered for symmetric thalamic involvement — “Acute demyelinating encephalomyelitis and multiple sclerosis may lead to bilateral thalamic lesions.”  
7. Metabolic disorders were considered as causes of bilateral thalamic signal changes — “Leigh syndrome, gangliosidoses, Krabbe’s disease, and Wilson’s disease can cause bilateral thalamic lesions.”  
8. Other rare conditions were considered in the differential — “Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (spongiform encephalopathy), thiamine deficiency (Wernicke’s encephalopathy), and Fahr’s disease (abnormal calcium deposits) can also be potential causes.”
